content: Jiagang Guo serves as a Technical Officer in the Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases at the World Health Organization (WHO) in Geneva, Switzerland. Jonathan King is a Scientist in the same department at WHO, also based in Geneva. Ornella Lincetto is a Medical Officer in the Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child & Adolescent Health & Ageing at WHO in Geneva. Pamela Sabina Mbabazi is a Medical Epidemiologist in the Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases at WHO, Geneva. Mwelecele Ntuli Malecela is the Director of the Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases at WHO, Geneva. Mohamed Jamsheed is a Regional Advisor for Vector-borne and Neglected Tropical Diseases at the WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia, located in New Delhi, India. Antonio Montresor is a Medical Officer in the Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases at WHO, Geneva. Pauline Mwinzi is a Medical Officer for the Expanded Special Project for Elimination of Neglected Tropical Diseases at the WHO Regional Office for Africa, based in Brazzaville, Congo. Piero Olliaro is the Unit Head of the Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases at WHO, Geneva. Shanthi Narayan Pal leads the Pharmacovigilance Team in the Department of Regulation and Prequalification at WHO, Geneva. Annette Martine Prüss-Ustün is a Scientist and Head of Policies & Interventions for Health & Environment in the Department of Environment, Climate Change, and Health at WHO, Geneva. Ruben Santiago Nicholls is a Regional Advisor for Neglected Infectious Diseases at the WHO Regional Office for the Americas/Pan American Sanitary Bureau in Washington, United States. Anthony Solomon is a Medical Officer in the Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases at WHO, Geneva. Supriya Warusavithana is a Regional Advisor for Neglected Tropical Diseases at the WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean in Cairo, Egypt. Rajpal Singh Yadav is a Scientist in the Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases at WHO, Geneva. Aya Yajima is a Technical Officer in the Division of Communicable Diseases at the WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific, based in Manila, Philippines. The external review group includes Dhekra A. Annuzaili, a Specialist Pediatrician and Independent Consultant based in Cairo, Egypt; Moses J. Chimbari, a Research Professor at the College of Health Sciences, University of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa; Alan Fenwick, a Professor of Tropical Parasitology and Founder of the Schistosomiasis Control Initiative Foundation in the United Kingdom; Hiroshi Ohmae, a Professor in the Department of Parasitology at the National Institute of Infectious Diseases in Tokyo, Japan; Winston A. Palasi, a National Programme Coordinator in the Disease Prevention and Control Bureau at the Department of Health in Manila, Philippines; Otavio S. Pieri, a Researcher at the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; Lorenzo Savioli, a Public Health Expert and Independent Consultant in Chavannes de Bogis, Switzerland; and Louis-Albert Tchuem Tchuenté, Coordinator of the National Program for the Control of Schistosomiasis and Soil-Transmitted Helminthiasis at the Ministry of Health in Yaoundé, Cameroon. The systematic review team includes Anthony Danso-Appiah, Paolo Eusebi, Eric Sam Loker, Charles Owuora Obonyo, and Liang Song. Liang Song has received research grants from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the National Science Foundation (NSF). The assessment concluded that no financial interests from funding sources could directly or apparently affect the professional judgment of the expert. The GRADE system was used to evaluate the quality of evidence. High-quality evidence indicates strong confidence that the true effect is close to the estimated effect. Moderate-quality evidence suggests the true effect is likely close to the estimate but may differ significantly. Low-quality evidence reflects limited confidence, with the true effect potentially differing substantially. Very low-quality evidence indicates minimal confidence, with the true effect likely differing significantly from the estimate. The impact of preventive chemotherapy on schistosomiasis morbidity was assessed through a systematic review and meta-analysis of 319 studies, including randomized trials and observational studies. The analysis focused on key age groups, such as preschool-aged children (pre-SAC), school-aged children (SAC), and adults. Preventive chemotherapy with praziquantel was associated with reductions in parasitological and morbidity outcomes, particularly in SAC and pre-SAC populations. However, data for adults and certain morbidity outcomes were limited or unavailable. The certainty of evidence for reducing prevalence was moderate, while it was low for morbidity outcomes. Further stratification by age group and Schistosoma species reduced the number of available studies, leading to imprecise estimates. The GDG also considered additional analyses on disease burden in pre-SAC populations and the safety and efficacy of praziquantel in young children. Other systematic reviews and meta-analyses examining the relationship between preventive chemotherapy and morbidity outcomes were also reviewed. These analyses highlighted the need for targeted interventions and further research to address gaps in evidence, particularly for specific age groups and morbidity outcomes.
